prompt: A factory's defect rate is $p = 0.10$. An inspector wants the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$ to be approximately normal, which requires the Large Counts condition: $np \ge 10$ and $n(1-p) \ge 10$. What is the smallest sample size $n$ that satisfies both?
hint: There are two conditions to meet. With a small $p$, think about which one is harder to satisfy: enough expected defects or enough expected good items?

hints.text: There are two conditions to meet. With a small $p$, think about which one is harder to satisfy: enough expected defects or enough expected good items?
Expected defects are the hard part, so solve $0.10n \ge 10$ for $n$. Then confirm that $0.90n \ge 10$ also holds at that value.
$n \ge 100$, and at $n = 100$ the counts are $np = 10$ and $n(1-p) = 90$, so the smallest sample size is $100$.

explanation: A normal approximation for $\hat{p}$ needs at least 10 expected successes and at least 10 expected failures.
The first condition, $np \ge 10$, becomes $0.1n \ge 10$, which gives $n \ge 100$.
The second condition, $n(1-p) \ge 10$, gives $0.9n \ge 10$, so $n \ge 11.1$, which is far easier to meet.
Both must hold, so the stricter one decides: the smallest sample size is $100$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Why the condition exists
steps: With $n = 50$, you expect only 5 defects; the count is piled up near 0 and skewed right, not bell-shaped.
With 10 or more expected defects, the distribution has room to spread out symmetrically.
Ten expected defects at a $10\%$ rate means 100 items.
